content_units: September 2026 Mini-Festival Concept: Cities at Night

A 6-film program built around nocturnal urban life, moving from seductive city spectacle to alienation, danger, romance, and finally a dreamlike farewell. The lineup mixes countries and decades so each weekend has its own mood while the full sequence feels like one long night deepening across cinema history.
Three-Weekend Screening Lineup
Weekend 1: The City as Seduction and Performance
Film 1: Night and the City (UK, 1950, dir. Jules Dassin)

A feverish London noir, this film turns the nighttime city into a maze of hustlers, wrestlers, promoters, and desperate ambition. Its slick pavements, backroom deals, and relentless forward motion make it an ideal opening statement for a festival about urban after-dark energy.
Film 2: Sweet Smell of Success (US, 1957, dir. Alexander Mackendrick)

Manhattan glitters here as a world of press agents, nightclub columns, and poisonous power, where every neon sign seems to hide a threat. The razor-sharp dialogue and hard-edged black-and-white photography deepen the theme by showing the city at night as glamorous, predatory theater.
Weekend 2: The City as Loneliness and Drift
Film 3: Le Samouraï (France, 1967, dir. Jean-Pierre Melville)

Melville’s Paris is stripped down to wet streets, metro shadows, and silent rooms, creating one of cinema’s great nocturnal cool worlds. The film’s precision and stillness shift the festival from bustling noir talkiness into a more isolated, existential kind of urban night.
Film 4: Taxi Driver (US, 1976, dir. Martin Scorsese)

New York becomes a lurid insomnia machine of steam, headlights, porno marquees, and psychic breakdown. By placing it after Le Samouraï, the program moves from controlled detachment to eruptive inner chaos while keeping the city nightscape central.
Weekend 3: The City as Desire, Memory, and Dream
Film 5: Chungking Express (Hong Kong, 1994, dir. Wong Kar-wai)

Hong Kong glows with snack bars, escalators, cramped apartments, and passing strangers, all rendered in a rush of color and longing. After the darkness of the earlier weekends, this film reintroduces speed and urban density in a lighter, more romantic register without losing the melancholy of nighttime solitude.
Film 6: After Hours (US, 1985, dir. Martin Scorsese)

This downtown New York odyssey turns one long night into a comic nightmare of wrong turns, strange encounters, and escalating unreality. It closes the festival beautifully because it gathers many of the series’ motifs—temptation, danger, loneliness, absurdity—into a single nocturnal spiral that feels both hilarious and haunted.
Why This Order Works on Screen

The sequence starts with muscular black-and-white noir, where the city is vivid, external, and socially crowded; it then narrows into cooler and more psychologically enclosed visions of urban night. By the final weekend, the palette opens into neon color and romantic drift before ending in a manic all-night fugue, giving the audience an emotional arc from excitement to dread to wistful, uncanny release.

Visually, the progression also avoids repetition: hard noir contrast leads into minimalist shadow, then grimy expressionist color, then pop-neon lyricism, and finally surreal downtown disorientation. Emotionally, that creates a satisfying rise and fall—hook the audience with classic noir propulsion, intensify with alienation and danger, then release with longing and dark comedy.
Host Notes for the Three Weekends
-   Weekend 1 pairing note:   Both films are sharp, talky, black-and-white studies in ambition and corruption, making the opening weekend feel polished and immediately accessible.
-   Weekend 2 pairing note:   These are the coldest and most psychologically pressurized entries, ideal for the middle slot when the festival can deepen and darken.
-   Weekend 3 pairing note:   The final weekend becomes more fluid, funny, and emotionally open, leaving viewers with the sensation of having wandered through many versions of the nighttime city.
